2026:UHC:3340
IN THE HIGH COURT OF UTTARAKHAND
AT NAINITAL
Bail Application 1st No. 130 of 2026
Salekh ......Applicant
Vs.
State of Uttarakhand .....Respondent
Presence:
Mr. Shashi Kant Shandilya, learned counsel assisted by Mr. Vishwaketu
Vaidya and Ms. Ruchi JJ learned counsel for the Applicant.
Mr. Chitrarth Kandpal, learned brief holder for the State of Uttarakhand.
Hon'ble Ashish Naithani, J (Oral)
The present bail application has been filed by the applicant
under Section 483 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita,
2023, seeking release on bail during trial in connection with FIR
No. 416 of 2025 dated 14.07.2025, registered under Sections 103(1)
and 61(2) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 at Police Station
Pathri, District Haridwar. It is stated to be the first bail application
before this Court, the earlier applications having been rejected,
including the second one by the learned Second Additional District
and Sessions Judge, Haridwar on 12.01.2026.
2. As per the State's case, the FIR was lodged on 14.07.2025
regarding the disappearance of the deceased, who had left his house
on the evening of 13.07.2025 for the purpose of transporting goods
but did not return. On the next day, his dead body was found in a
mango orchard area near Kishanpur, lying in the rear portion of his
1
Bail Application 1st No. 130 of 2026-----Salekh vs State of Uttarakhand
Ashish Naithani J.

e-rickshaw, with a ligature mark around the neck indicating
strangulation. The mobile phone of the deceased was not found at
the spot.
3. During investigation, the involvement of the present applicant
surfaced along with a co-accused, who is the wife of the deceased.
The State alleges that both were in a relationship and had conspired
to eliminate the deceased. It is alleged that the deceased was called
on the pretext of transporting mango crates, taken towards a
secluded orchard area, and was administered intoxicants, after
which he was strangulated using a cloth. It is further alleged that
certain articles of the deceased, including personal belongings,
were thrown into a drain.
4. The applicant was arrested on 16.07.2025 from Laksar Railway
Station. At the time of arrest, a mobile phone and cash were
allegedly recovered from his possession. Subsequently, on his
pointing out, certain articles of the deceased were stated to have
been recovered from bushes near a drain, while the mobile phone of
the deceased could not be recovered.
5. Upon completion of investigation, charge-sheet dated 01.10.2025
has been submitted against the applicant and co-accused under
Sections 103(1) and 61(2) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023.
6. Heard learned counsel for the parties and perused the records.
7. Learned counsel for the applicant submits that the applicant has
been falsely implicated in the present case on the basis of mere
suspicion and there is no direct or cogent evidence connecting him
with the alleged offence. It is argued that the entire State case rests
on circumstantial evidence, which is weak in nature and the chain
of circumstances is not complete.
8. It is further submitted that there is no eyewitness to the alleged
incident and even the FIR does not name the present applicant,
thereby making his subsequent implication doubtful. Learned
2
Bail Application 1st No. 130 of 2026-----Salekh vs State of Uttarakhand
Ashish Naithani J.

counsel contends that no recovery of any weapon, blood-stained
clothes or any other incriminating article has been effected from the
possession of the applicant.
9. Learned counsel next submits that the alleged motive of illicit
relationship is wholly baseless and unsupported by any reliable
evidence. Mere call detail records, it is argued, do not establish
either such relationship or the presence of the applicant at the place
of occurrence.
10. It is also argued that the alleged confessional statements
before the police are inadmissible in evidence and cannot be relied
upon against the applicant. Further, the post-mortem report also
does not conclusively connect the applicant with the alleged crime.
11. Lastly, it is submitted that the applicant is a law-abiding
citizen having no criminal antecedents and there is no likelihood of
his absconding or misusing the liberty of bail. On these grounds, it
is prayed that the applicant be enlarged on bail during the pendency
of trial.
12. Per contra, learned State counsel vehemently opposes the bail
application and submits that the investigation in the present case
has been completed and charge-sheet has already been filed against
the applicant and co-accused, which prima facie establishes their
involvement in the commission of the offence.
13. It is submitted that the statements of material witnesses
recorded during investigation support the State's case. Learned
State counsel further contends that the applicant was arrested on the
basis of credible information and, on his pointing out, recovery of
the weapon used in the crime as well as the mobile phone and voter
ID card of the deceased has been effected.
14. It is further argued that the inquest report and post-mortem
report corroborate the State's story and clearly indicate homicidal
death. The State also relies upon the motive of illicit relationship
3
Bail Application 1st No. 130 of 2026-----Salekh vs State of Uttarakhand
Ashish Naithani J.

between the applicant and the wife of the deceased, which led to the
commission of the offence.
15. Considering the gravity and seriousness of the offence, it is
contended by the learned State counsel that the applicant does not
deserve to be enlarged on bail and the bail application is liable to be
rejected.
16. Upon perusal of the post-mortem report pertaining to the
deceased, this Court finds that the cause of death has been opined
as "asphyxia due to strangulation," which prima facie indicates a
homicidal death.
17. The report records the presence of rigor mortis throughout the
body along with fixed post-mortem lividity, and estimates the time
since death to be approximately twelve to twenty-four hours prior
to the examination. The presence of petechial haemorrhages,
cyanosis, and bluish discolouration of the extremities and facial
region are noted, which are consistent with asphyxial death.
18. A ligature mark has been observed around the neck,
described as irregular in nature with variation in width at different
points. The internal examination reveals findings such as a
localized hematoma in the laryngeal region and fracture of the
hyoid bone, which prima facie indicate compression of the neck
structures.
19. However, the description of the ligature mark as irregular and
overlapping in nature assumes significance in the absence of any
material placed on record to establish correlation between the said
mark and the alleged ligature (gamcha) stated to have been used in
the commission of the offence.
20. It is also not in dispute that no report from the Forensic
Science Laboratory, examining the said ligature material for any
biological or trace evidence, has been brought on record. At this
4
Bail Application 1st No. 130 of 2026-----Salekh vs State of Uttarakhand
Ashish Naithani J.

stage, therefore, the alleged weapon of offence remains
uncorroborated by scientific evidence.
21. The post-mortem report further records the presence of
seminal discharge. While such a phenomenon may occur in cases of
asphyxial death, no material has been placed before this Court to
indicate that any scientific or serological examination in this regard
was conducted during investigation.
22. The report also notes the presence of partially digested food
material in the stomach and intestines. However, no correlation
between the same and the estimated time of death has been
demonstrated from the material available on record.
23. The State has placed reliance upon the alleged recovery of a
checkered cotton cloth (gamcha) along with certain personal
belongings of the deceased, purportedly recovered on the pointing
out of the applicant from bushes near a drain.
24. It is noticed that the said recovery has not been witnessed by
any independent public witness, and the recovery memo reflects
that the witnesses are police personnel. While the evidentiary value
of such recovery is a matter for trial, its nature assumes relevance at
this stage when the case rests on circumstantial evidence.
25. Further, no material has been placed on record to show that
the recovered cloth was subjected to any forensic examination so as
to establish the presence of blood, DNA, or any other trace
evidence linking it either with the deceased or with the applicant. In
the absence of such scientific corroboration, the evidentiary weight
of the recovery remains a matter of scrutiny.
26. It is also noted that the mobile phone of the deceased, which
is stated to have been disposed of in the drain, could not be
recovered despite search. The non-recovery of such a potentially
relevant piece of evidence also forms part of the overall factual
matrix, which shall be examined during trial. The absence of any
5
Bail Application 1st No. 130 of 2026-----Salekh vs State of Uttarakhand
Ashish Naithani J.

FSL report renders the recovery of the gamcha an unscientifically
corroborated piece of evidence, and its evidentiary worth at trial
will have to be assessed with due circumspection by the Trial
Court.
27. Furthermore, the mobile phone of the deceased, which the
applicant allegedly disclosed he had also thrown into the drain
along with the gamcha and the voter ID card, could not be
recovered despite extensive search on the night of 16.07.2025 and
again on the morning of 17.07.2025. While the State explains this
by the strong water current in the drain, the non-recovery of a
crucial piece of evidence that could have contained Call Detail
Records, messages, and other electronically stored information
relevant to establishing the alleged conspiracy, is another gap in the
forensic chain.
28. The State has placed reliance on the alleged confessional
statements of the applicant and co-accused recorded by the
Investigating Officer at the police station. It is a settled position of
law that any confession made to a police officer is inadmissible as
substantive evidence under the BharatiyaSakshyaAdhiniyam, 2023,
except to the limited extent of discovery of a fact. Even such
limited admissibility is contingent upon the discovery being duly
corroborated by independent and reliable evidence. In the present
case, the alleged recovery is not supported by any forensic or
independent corroboration, thereby diminishing its evidentiary
value at this stage.
29. The contention raised on behalf of the applicant that no
confessional statement was made further adds to the uncertainty
surrounding such material. In any event, the statement attributed to
the co-accused, having been made before the police, is equally
inadmissible against the applicant and cannot be treated as
substantive evidence.
6
Bail Application 1st No. 130 of 2026-----Salekh vs State of Uttarakhand
Ashish Naithani J.

30. Thus, at this stage, the State's case, shorn of such
inadmissible material, rests primarily on other evidence collected
during investigation, which shall be subject to appreciation during
trial.
31. The State's case of conspiracy is founded substantially on the
alleged illicit relationship between the applicant and co-accused
Reena, the call records between the parties, and the alleged
agreement to eliminate the deceased. However, the charge sheet
itself acknowledges that CDR reports from the telecom companies
had been sought but had not been received at the time of filing of
the charge sheet, and would be forwarded to the Court upon receipt.
No CDR report has been placed before this Court either. The
applicant is not named in the original FIR, which was lodged
against unknown accused persons. His implication at a later stage,
primarily on the basis of statements of co-accused Reena and his
own alleged disclosure statement, raises the concern pointed out by
the learned counsel for the applicant that the applicant's
involvement is a result of subsequent suspicion rather than direct
evidence.
32. Furthermore, no recovery of any blood-stained clothing, no
fingerprint evidence, no DNA evidence, no CCTV footage, and no
independent eyewitness connects the applicant with the scene of
occurrence. The post-mortem report does not describe any trace
evidence or transfer material found on the body of the deceased that
could point to the applicant.
33. The applicant is stated to have no criminal antecedents. The
investigation is complete and the charge sheet has been filed. Trial
has not yet commenced. It is relevant to note that the applicant has
been in custody since 16.07.2025, i.e., for a period of
approximately nine months as of the date of this judgment.
7
Bail Application 1st No. 130 of 2026-----Salekh vs State of Uttarakhand
Ashish Naithani J.

34. In view of the foregoing discussion, this Court is of the
considered opinion that the present case is one where bail can be
granted with appropriate conditions, for the following principal
reasons.
35. The State's case, as it stands on the basis of admissible
evidence, is founded entirely on circumstantial evidence. The chain
of circumstances, as it emerges from the material on record, is not
so complete and unbroken as to preclude every reasonable
hypothesis consistent with the innocence of the applicant. The
absence of any FSL report on the gamcha, the absence of DNA or
biological evidence linking the applicant to the crime, the absence
of any independent eyewitness, the absence of corroborated CDR
evidence, the inadmissibility of the confessional statements, and the
significant lacunae including the unexplained finding of passage of
semen and the absence of any trace evidence examination,
collectively create a situation where the prima facie case against the
applicant, while not absent, is not of such an overwhelming
character as would disentitle him to bail during the lengthy trial that
lies ahead.
36. The gravity of the charge offence under Section 103(1) of the
B.N.S. is not lost on this Court, and bail is not being granted
mechanically or as a matter of course. However, this Court is
guided by the principle, repeatedly affirmed by the Supreme Court
of India, that bail is the rule and jail is the exception, and that pre-trial detention is not meant to serve as punishment for an unproved
offence.
ORDER
In view of the aforesaid, the bail application of the applicant
Salekh is hereby allowed.
8
Bail Application 1st No. 130 of 2026-----Salekh vs State of Uttarakhand
Ashish Naithani J.

Accordingly, the Applicant Salekh, son of Ilmchand, resident
of Village Ambuwala, Police Station Pathri, District Haridwar,
shall be released on bail in connection with FIR No. 416 of 2025,
under Sections 103(1) and 61(2) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita,
2023, Police Station Pathri, District Haridwar, on his furnishing a
personal bond of Rs. 75,000/- (Rupees Seventy five thousand only)
along with two reliable sureties of the like amount each to the
satisfaction of the Trial Court.
It is clarified that any observation made hereinabove is
only for the purpose of deciding the present bail application and
shall not be construed as an expression on the merits of the case,
and the Trial Court shall proceed independently, uninfluenced by
any such observations.
(Ashish Naithani, J.)
Dated: 29.04.2026
NR/
